extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants, peer reviewers, biomedical researchers and policy observers interested in NIH peer review changes
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and critiquing NIH's Simplified Peer Review Framework: how criteria are reorganized, how scoring changes (1-9 for two criteria), and whether the change will reduce reputation bias in funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of the Research (Significance + Innovation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The new framework combines Significance and Innovation into one 'Importance of the Research' box, scored 1-9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to 'minimize the tyranny of the current Innovation criterion.' The framework removes the obligation to separately address Innovation, but reviewers who prioritize innovation can still lower overall impact scores; combining the two does not force reviewers to change how they weigh innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor and Feasibility (Approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: The old 'Approach' criterion is rendered as 'Rigor and Feasibility' and will receive a 1-9 score under the new framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of the two scored dimensions under the simplified framework. No additional scoring or integration rules are imposed beyond the 1-9 numeric rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator/Environment adequacy (adequate/not adequate dropdown; unscored)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigator and Environment criteria are placed into a simple adequate/not adequate dropdown menu and are unscored (but will contribute to overall impact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although converted to an adequacy checkbox rather than a numeric score, these items 'will contribute to the overall impact.' The blog notes this may reduce snide comments about Investigator/Environment but argues it does not change how reviewers think about or allow such views to influence overall impact scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall Impact score and integration of criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers still produce an overall impact score and are not obliged to integrate the scored and unscored criteria into that score in any particular manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because there is no required method for integrating scored (Importance; Rigor/Feasibility) and unscored (Investigator/Environment adequacy) items into the overall impact, the framework does not force a change in reviewer behavior; unscored items may still inform overall impact at reviewers' discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring mechanics: two numeric criteria on a 1-9 scale
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplified approach produces a 1-9 score for two criteria: Importance of the Research and Rigor and Feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit procedural change in how numeric scores are assigned — fewer scored dimensions. The blog implies this is intended to reduce influence of reputation and innovation-focused weighting, but notes limitations because reviewer discretion remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for explicit measures to detect/reduce reputation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: If the framework's goal is to 'reduce the potential for general scientific reputation to have an undue influence,' NIH must define and track measures of that bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested measurement approaches include: tracking before/after funding outcomes; calculating institution-level success rates adjusted for submission volume/size ('measures of success rate to account for larger and more vigorous grant-submitting institutions’ statistical advantage'); surveying reviewers about perceived reputation and matching responses to institutional outcomes; and examining individual PI reputation effects. The blog criticizes NIH for not specifying how 'bias' will be measured and doubts NIH will perform thorough data-driven evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional/top-funded recipient analysis as part of bias assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying 'top-funded recipient organizations' is a starting point for probing institutional reputational bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog notes these organizations are already identified but argues NIH must 'probe a lot deeper' — e.g., control for submission volume and vigor, and distinguish statistical advantage from reputational advantage. This is presented as a procedural/analytical standard NIH should apply when evaluating the framework's effects.
